projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Lawrence McCulloch was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay, we're going to go ahead and get started. Bear with me, this is not my normal thing, but we're going to start the Veteran's History Project. We're going to do the interview of Lawrence McCulloch. My name is Kristin Anderson and I am affiliated with the National Court Reporters Association. We are short interviewers today so I'm in the interviewing capacity instead of the court-reporter capacity. So, we have Lawrence here, and the location of where we are today is at the [address redacted]. Okay. So, Lawrence, we're going to get started.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: First we want to ask you about -- tell us where you were born? What year and where you were born?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Born in the city -- I was born in 1926 [birth date redacted].

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: [Birth date redacted]. Oh, you have a birthday coming up pretty soon?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I'll be 90.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Congratulations.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I told people a few years ago I never thought I would reach 90. When I hit it, I got a bottle of whiskey in my room -- but I ain't -- I've had it for three or four years, I ain't never opened it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: It's good just to know it's there in case you need it.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: With the medicine, you know, I have -- I looked at it. I've had my good days -- good days -- and bad days.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So, Lawrence, tell us who were your parents and what were their occupations?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Farmers.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Farmers? That's great.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Frank McCulloch and Andi McCulloch, my mother.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Great. And we talked a little bit before we went on the record about how many siblings you had. So tell us about your siblings, how many -- how many boys and girls?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I got two sons.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What about your siblings, your brothers and sister? -- we'll talk about them in a little bit.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I've got eight brothers and one sister.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Great.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But it's just me and one brother and sister is all that's left.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, wow. Okay. Yeah, the baby's the sister, right?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Do you -- do you want to share the names? Can you remember the name of all your siblings?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Frankie, Raymond, Clarence, Richard, Leroy, Walter, me, Johnny and Alton. The sister is the baby, Dorothy.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's the next thing I wanted to ask you about, which of them served in the military?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Six of them.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Six?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Six of -- well actually, seven. Seven.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Just my oldest brother, next to the brother -- youngest brother didn't go in the service. My oldest brother do the -- what do you call it? They had there the deferment to help on a farm. They had some of those during World War II to help -- if he wasn't left to farm, my -- the military wouldn't have nothing to eat.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right. Exactly. The backbone of America, right?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So what were you doing before you entered the service?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I just got out of high school.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Wow. Did you get drafted or --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I graduated May. In June I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I could have went later. I signed up and they told me: Go home, we'll call you in 30 to 90 days. I ain't ready to go in thirty, I'm ready to go now. I was out of Dodgefeld (ph). They said: Go through that door. Hold your hand up. You're in. There wasn't any use to go back to the farm, so they were going to call me within thirty days. I said: Why fool around? I'm out there. Next week I'm in Camp Roberts California, taking seven weeks infantry training. Then they took me over to Santiago, the Navy base, give us six weeks, two weeks of amphibious training, and trained us for beach landing in the Pacific. But I was sure glad they changed orders. They needed us in Europe so they put us on a troop train and sent us across country, put us on a ship, sent us to Europe. I'm in combat over there in Europe. I hate those ship rides. Can't take them. I get seasick. I get -- I mean -- sick. Some of them guys, I tell you, I thought -- some of them I know they lost 8 or 10 pounds on -- yeah, 22-day voyage. We had -- we had a British ship took us across. They fed us two meals a day, sweat the chow line out 6 to 8 hours for an hour. You get through, you get out of line, you have to get in line for another. Two meals for 18 days. You talk about a bunch of GIs fussing.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: When you enlisted, which branch of the military did you enlist in?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I didn't have no choice, when I got graduated, I got my greetings from Uncle Sam.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: You were ready to go very quickly?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I was eighteen when I graduated.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So you were drafted into the Army or Air Force?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Army.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And then --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: After three years in the Army, I got out and joined the Air Force Reserves; and two years later, in 1950, I was called to active duty in the Air Force, so I stayed 24 years in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: When you just said that you were on the boat heading over to Europe, was that when you were in the Army?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I was -- right. My first -- I made two trips overseas in the Army, by ship.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Then when I went to the Pacific, though, in the Air Force, we flew.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Of course. There you go. That was a very nice switch I bet?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But to show you how unlucky I was when I went to the Pacific, I had to go on a military plane. I didn't get -- to come back, I come on them -- what do you call it? -- them civilian airlines where they had these hostesses serving us food. But when I went the first time, I was with a bunch of GIs serving us GI food.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, goodness. So you didn't get to choose, you were just drafted into the Army?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I knew I was going to be drafted, so I just --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Went ahead and did it?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: -- got it over with.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. Got you. Okay. So did you pick the Army originally?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I didn't have no choice.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. Then you kind of already talked a little bit about this. You departed for training camp, so can you tell us a little bit about your early days a little bit again, about how you were -- your training before you were sent oversees, so you --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I took seven weeks of infantry training in Camp Robert, and then we went and joined my division and went to San Diego and took amphibious training a couple of weeks, got throwed in the Guard House for fighting the Navy, spent my first night in the Guard House in the military. Anyways, they put us on a train and sent us to New York, put us on a ship, sent to us Europe, and the next month we were in combat.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That all happened very fast.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Seasick the whole -- I couldn't -- it wasn't just me, it was two-thirds of the people.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Do you remember your instructors back then? I know we talked about, a little bit, that you kind of did some training, too.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But it's hard to remember some of them in World War II.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What were they like?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Well, when -- during the World War II and infantry, I was lucky, this officer -- we had a captain -- he was a West Pointer. He was good. He went by the book, and that's what he expected you to do; and some of them guys that been messing up, they didn't take him long to straighten them out.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: I bet not.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: If you are going to do it, do it right.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Did you have any specialized training after that, after you went over -- I know you said you had the seven weeks, but did you have any special --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: When I got out of the Army, in the last of '47 and joined the Air Force Reserve, for two years I went to work as a machinist, sheet metal wielding, under the GI Bill and for two years I learned the machinist sheet-metal trade. So I was in the Air Force Reserve, and in 1950 they called me to active duty, and I took typing in school, so when they called me to active duty, they put me in finance, typing up payrolls. And I told the officer, I said, Man, this ain't my field, you know. So after about two or three months fooling around with that deal they had a meeting at the club and this sergeant, he was looking for personnel for the flight line and I told him what I been doing so I got transferred to machine shop/sheet metal and from then on that's all I did in the military.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Wow. Okay. That's neat. Well, when you first went in, how -- I know you said you knew you were going to be drafted and so you went ahead and signed right up?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: How was it to adapt to military life? Like the physical regimen? The barracks? The food? Social life?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I done had five brothers ahead of me. They told me everything.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: They told you everything?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And if y'all don't remember, but before the war, things were rough out here. I mean, people were hurting. They were going to parade lines, food rations. Things were rough. Actually, I hate to say it, but the war was really good in a way, but we lost a lot of man.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yes, we sure did.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But it put the country back on its feet, I think; and if you read the history, I think you'll agree with me.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: We do. That's right.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Because y'all don't remember, it was hurting back in the late 30s. People didn't have nothing.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No jobs. No food.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. I don't know who used to joke about the good old days: Which ones?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Well, it makes you appreciate everything you have.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So we -- when you -- so now we are going to talk a little bit about your service when you went into battle. Where -- so you -- where did you serve at in Europe when you got sent over on the ship?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: We went into combat in -- I guess just before we got into Germany, into Belgium, into Belgium into Germany.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What are some of your memories about that experience, getting over there into battle?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: It's crazy. Them -- what do you call them? We called them the square heads, the Germans -- shelling us with them 88s and we're shelling them back with the artillery. And what we had -- you know, we had them earplugs. So the artillery shells was firing behind us but half the time we didn't know where they was at, that's the reason I got hearing aids on now. I was too hard headed. Them hearing aids were -- what do you call them back there then -- they were horrible. We were really having hearing trouble when you wear them.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: I think so.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But I wish I would have wore them.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So you were in the front lines then, when you were in battle?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I could dig a fox hole pretty good, but, you know, I was just 18. I was -- maybe I shouldn't say it, but we had guys 37, 38 years old up there in the front lines with us. I was just -- and you couldn't help but feeling sorry for them at -- to me, I thought 37, 38 was old when I was 18. When I got 38, I didn't think it was.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right. You never do. It always seems younger.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But I had to feel sorry for them -- well, a bunch of them from the city. And they were -- I got to learn a lot from them, you know. I don't know whether y'all would remember, but before the war, we had depression, people didn't have jobs, and the division I joined, 86, most of them were National Guards from Chicago. And we used to joke with them, we were farmers, and you know what they used to tell us: Y'all growed y'alls food. We had to steal ours during the depression. I hadn't thought about it, but they didn't have no food. They said we had to steal it. I never will forget that.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: We thought we had it rough.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So, when you were over there in combat, witnessing all the destruction and the casualties -- I mean, how did that make you feel?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I don't know. It was crazy. I got shafted -- I'm left handed.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And when we attacked the town, some of the guys go to the left side of the building and others right, so guess where I'm at? -- on the left. Most of the time I was leading the other eight or ten guys and we get -- you get the first enemy fire, you know; but they learn fast, the Germans, that they had guys coming from the left side. There, for the most, they hit from the right side of the building but we ended up going both sides. And like a dummy in basic, I was taking basic training, they put us out there on the bazooka -- you know what a bazooka is? For knocking out these tanks -- so like a dummy, they were pulling a fake tank, the tank with no engine which a cable on it, pulling it about 50, 70 miles an hour, 150, 75 yards and we would fire the bazooka to qualify it. So, like a dummy, I thought, well I'm doing my job, I hit the tank every time. So when I joined my division, guess what happened, they said: You're the bazooka man. If I had thought about it ahead of time, I would have missed every time.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, goodness. So, being over there in that experience, what kind of friendships and camaraderie did you have with men over there?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: They stuck together fast. They helped each other out real fast because they -- well, you hate to say it this way, in combat, the more bodies you got close to you -- I mean, you hate to say it this way, but that's what you got. Maybe the bullet will hit him and not you. I mean, that's -- what else can you do? You hate to admit it, but --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Survival?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But don't tell me there's too many that did admit it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, I bet not. While you were there, how did you stay in touch with your family and friends back here?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: We didn't get too much mail. They had them little -- what did they call them -- them little V-mails. You couldn't write but a few lines.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Like a postcard?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Like a little card, yeah.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. So what did you do for recreation when you were off duty? Did you have much off-duty time?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Not much. Not much. I know one thing, when the war was over, we rounded up -- in a few weeks -- rounded up them German prisoners, then we was one of four of those divisions were coming back to the states to go to the Pacific. We had to leave out of combat and we camped about ten miles -- eight or ten miles out of Paris and put up our tents, got -- so on Monday morning they were going to haul us into Paris. They were on the Seine River by the Eiffel Tower. They dropped us off at one o'clock -- I never will forget this here. That was the greatest life I had -- they dropped us off at one o'clock. They said, We'll be back every day at one o'clock to pick you up and take you back. If you ain't back the following Monday, you're AWOL. I made it back the following Monday. I spent those seven days. And I didn't smoke and I lined my jacket -- the jacket we had -- I had -- a guy in the outfit was a tailor. I had him -- got an oversized one and had him where I could line it with them cigarettes because them cigarettes, after the war, were like gold because the people didn't have nothing to eat and I understood cigarettes took care of the appetite, and I had it -- I had it made with them cigarettes. But my buddies kept wanting me to give them cigarettes. I said, You guys are crazy, not when I can go into town and live it up.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Where were you when the war ended?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: We were down in Austria. We ended up out of Vienna, Austria.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And how did you get back home?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: We come back by ship.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: A ship. Over by ship and back by ship?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Seasick every time. Then I went back over again by ship and come back last '40 to '46 by ship.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So when you got back over here, how were you received from your family and the community?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: They were great. Most of them were great.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Do you remember that experience when you got back after the war?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Some of it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Did you come over -- when you came by ship, did you dock in New York or where did you dock?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Yeah, we docked in New York. They got us a -- well, at that time you didn't have flights. You come on a train.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right. Okay. So you took a train?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And them trains, the one we came -- coming back after the war, coming back home here, the ones going back carrying troops had priority. They would have to cut us off a track and delay us sometimes for hours, but they had priority over us.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: I guess --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I know a lot of guys, they used to fuss. What are you going to do? They've got -- I said, we need them guys over there in combat more than we need to be home, so that's the way they looked at it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So did you have a -- did they receive you when you docked in New York at the port? Did they -- was there a lot of people there?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah. They had the girls and everything out there. It was a great deal, really.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's nice.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Had a band and everything.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, that's neat.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And the only problem, close by was some WACs.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: The Air Force?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: The Army women. Women. A few of them invited us over to their barracks, and I never will forget, we ended up in a little -- they had to call the Military Police and I ended up that night in the guard house for a while -- well, they invited us over to have a good time, that's what we were doing. And you couldn't blame them. They had been up -- you know.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So what about, too, when you -- after you got back and you came back to Texas on the train, did you have a good -- did they realize those were military servicemen or were you with other civilians on the train, or did you get a good welcome?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Very few civilians were on the train with us.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So did you get back here in San Antonio? Is that where -- where you got off the train when you got back?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Right. And I got, I guess, a 20-day leave, I guess. Then I reported back to Fort Sam.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And then when I was turning back in, my brother came out of prison camp, and just before my 30-day (sic) leave was over, about ten days before -- a week before it was over, he came home, out of prison. I hadn't seen him in a few years. And he seen my patch. He said: You guys was the division that freed us. I remember we freed the American prisoners but we didn't know -- we didn't have time. We give them our rations and our cigarettes and kept going because there was three or -- three weeks of war left. He knows my patch. He said: You guys are the ones that freed us. That's how close we were.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What was on your patch?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: 86 Black Hawk Division.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. That's great. Wow.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: He seen that and, You guys were -- all we did was we give them our rations and cigarettes and had to keep going.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So when you got back, then you had to readjust to civilian life and I know you had to transition, so you were back here --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Well, I went back to Europe for two years.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Again? After that leave, then you went back again?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I went for the last part of '45 to '47. I went to Europe, had it -- lived it up.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: You know what I ended up doing?

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I got over the center there and I took typing in school. I don't know why.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I think I know why, because we got to get in the class with the girls, typing. But anyways, so they find out I typed so they sent me to Vienna, Austria, down there.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And that's where you were?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Running the Teletype machine, sending messages to Italy, Germany, Austria, you know. I had it made.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, you did. And so that's where you were?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And them cigarettes, we got a carton of cigarettes every week for 50 cents, and I didn't smoke. Guess what I could do with them outside on the black market?

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: I bet you did well.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: $200. But I couldn't send that money home, but man, could I have fun. And my buddies that smoked, they expected me to give them cigarettes. I said, Hell, you guys are crazy. I'll never have this golden opportunity again in my life.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's great.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I could. But them people, you know I found out later, they didn't have food and a cigarette helped their hunger.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right. So when you -- do you have any veterans that you still keep in contact that you served with?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No, most all of them are gone. About two years ago the last few that I knew checked out, because I was the young -- I was the youngest.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Obviously at 18.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: But did you have some that you kept in touch with for years?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Yeah, I had a few.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Where were they located?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I had one guy in Oklahoma and one good buddy in California. I had one down in Alabama, I think.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Wow. Did you ever get together or anything after the war?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No. No. Never got together.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And so do you belong to any of the veterans organizations?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No. I joined one there for a while and then that wasn't my goose.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: It wasn't your thing? Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I couldn't see going. All they want to do is talk about -- you know, I had enough of it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, I bet. So --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But the biggest problem I got into when I come back -- went back to Oklahoma, after my ten-day extension on my leave here of -- my brother got me the leave. I got back to Oklahoma to join my division. They done shipped out to the Pacific.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So then what happened?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: So that ten-day extension I got saved my life. I didn't have -- my division had to go into combat in the Pacific. They had to make a beached landing. So, anyways, I headed up there -- had it made up in Oklahoma, being a veteran there in June. It was very few World War II veterans back in the states. Most of them was in Europe or in the Pacific, and I'm up there with all of them ribbons on and -- and the Major, I never will forget, he said -- I was in car pool then. He said, We need somebody on over in the -- they had horses to ride for the dependents, for the officers' wives and their kids. He said, We need somebody to take care of the -- you were raised on a farm? I said, Yeah, I know all about cattle, horses. He said, We need somebody to take charge -- take them horses, to saddle them and everything. So I ended up over -- I had a detail and the first week I'm over there and this Major, he had a 17-year-old daughter. She was -- she thought -- he let me date her. And it was about five miles into town, in Muskogee, Oklahoma, and on a few times on Saturday evening, he would let me ride the bus in with her and we would go to a movie and eat and come back, but no -- nothing else.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So, getting a little bit back, we kind of talked a little off the record before we got started. You said that you were doing some training. You did seven-week training. How did that fall into your military service when you were doing -- I think you said three years of --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: That was basic training.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: In basic training?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Right. It was training with the A1 rifle and -- what do you call it -- hand grenades.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And you were in charge of the training?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No, I was -- I was just the PI on the end.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So tell us, after you got back, then you said -- at what point did you go into -- were you in the Air Force?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I got out of the Army the last part of '47 and then the first -- in January, I think '48, I joined the Air Force Reserves.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yes?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I didn't want no more. And then, in 1950 the Korean War broke out. I got called for active duty in the Air Force and stayed for 24 years in the Air Force. I wasn't -- it was so much easier than the Army.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And while I was out there two years, I learned the machine/sheet metal trade and that's what I got into in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So after you were sent over for the Korean War, then you came back at some point and then you went into the machine shop?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No, I went into -- when I went into the Air Force in 1950, I got in the shop right away.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right away. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: It was just during that time. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Then I went to Viet -- I went over there, to Korea, and I came back in '55 -- and I'm trying to think now.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: In '57, in Korea, I was in the shops.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: You were in the shops there too? Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And when I came back in '57, I was out at Brooks Air Force Base in the ensignman shop, and they found my records where I was in the Army. So they was having trouble with them two- and three-striper drill instructors at Lackland, so guess what happened to me -- they shipped me over there to go to six weeks instructor school to be a drilling sergeant training them basic. I spent '57, '58, and '59 over there training them basics.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's where that comes in. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I didn't like it, but -- you know -- but the Major we had -- a guy would lose his flight, and what made a couple of us other guys mad, he wouldn't punish the Sergeant that couldn't handle his flight, he would give it to us and we would have to try to straighten it out for him. So I went up -- after I was there a couple of years training, we had to redo some of our barracks, so we moved up to the WAF area and used the certain section of the WAF area. But the problem up there were -- we had in our barracks -- they were open base. Up there the WAFs had four to a room. So we tried to train them guys four to a room but all them girls, the instructors, were women, you know, and the officers, you know, and they begged me for months to transfer to train them WAFs but only one requirement, you had to get your wife's permission.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: How did that go?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I didn't even ask. I was glad I got out of that.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: When did you get married along the way?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I got married in '49, while I was out of the service.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. During that time. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But I was -- when I was over as a GI, when I was up there in that WAF area where we had our barracks, I got to know some of those instructors. But maybe I shouldn't tell you this here -- every now and then they would con me into going into their WAF barracks to inspect -- maybe I shouldn't say this. At the end of the door, the lady -- you know, the guard, if there was a male in the barrack, she would say: Male in the barracks, to let them other girls, in, and a few times I went in to check, to inspect, they hollered: Male in the barracks. Guess what happened? A couple of them young girls would come down the hall just with a towel around the waist.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, goodness.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Well, you couldn't blame them, I guess. But the bad part, we would go out on the parade field to march, guess who won all the time? The WAFs. Well, the women had coordinated two or three years earlier than we. They would make us look sick marching out there.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So after that, was it 24 years? Is that what you said, or how many years did you work?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: In the Air Force, 24. I retired in '74.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. So after separating from the military, tell us a little bit about where you ended up.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: After my oldest brother was on the farm -- we had 80 acres, and all my other brothers were gone; mother and parents are all gone, so I went out there and went into the cattle business. Me -- I got a tractor and had 20 head of cattle and a bull. I got in the cattle business off and on for about fifteen years.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Made some pretty good money. But I had -- I couldn't do -- I had some friends, when they retired, some of them they did nothing. I had to do something. I still, to this day, I got to do something. I can't -- I wish sometimes I could just do nothing.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Well, it keeps the mind alert, don't you think?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Oh, I guess. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What did -- at what point were you involved with the astronauts and stuff?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: When I was out at Brooks.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: At Brooks?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Working in -- I worked in them chambers and I got to know -- I had to -- I worked in the shops, machine shop, ensignmen, sheet metal, wielding and adonizing, had a glass blower from Germany over there and a typewriter, all in one shop --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: -- we had. And we got to work with all them people.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: So I got to working with quite a few of them doing a bunch of --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Projects. Yeah. So, little bit -- we can talk a little bit now about some of your reflections. How did the wartime experiences affect your life, do you think?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I don't know. Well, it -- I guess it made me realize how well off we are here. People don't realize how well off we are until they get -- see them people suffering like a bunch of -- nothing to eat.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But it don't do no good to try to explain it to somebody unless they actually see it, then they can understand it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah, that's true.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But most of it they understand it pretty good, but some of them, yeah, one ear and out the other.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. So did you have like any life lesson that you would want to share to anybody looking at this?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Not really. I mean, I've -- like -- like I always tell people, I feel pretty lucky. You hear me complaining very little. And why do some people complain all the time? You've got some, they've got to complain. We used to always use that old expression, Some people would bitch if they was hung with a new rope. You've heard that saying, and I believe some of them would.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So I think I kind of know, maybe, how you'll answer this question, but how did your military service impact your feelings about war and the military in general? I mean, you were pretty excited about: Well, I'm going to get drafted anyway. I'm here to sign up -- but looking back, how do you think it's impacted your feelings about war and the military?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Well, I looked at it this way: We had to protect our country, so the country had to come first. Now, you still got a lot of people that don't think that way, but most of us do.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's right.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: If you know that most of us do.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. What do you -- what kind of message would you like to leave to future generations that like?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: That's a good question. I don't have no idea.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: That's okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I don't know how to word it.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So thinking about everything we've been talking about, is there anything we haven't discussed that we should add, like --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I don't think. I think you covered everything pretty thoroughly.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: We did. Okay. I think we did talk -- I mean, I mentioned that you got married in '49 and you were starting to tell me about your sons. Why don't you tell us a little bit about them. I think you said they were in the service?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I think -- let's see, I'm trying to think now. My first son was born in '53.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: What was his name -- or what's his name?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: The other one was born in '55.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Both of them spent military. Both of them. One went -- one is the Army and one in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So both of your alma maters?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: My youngest son -- my two brothers, after they got out of the war, they went in the truck-driving business and my youngest son, that's what he wanted to do. So when he got out of school, he wanted to be a truck driver so I sent him to truck-driver school. I told him, I said, at 18, they ain't going to hire you. He said I want to be a truck driver. I sent him to school up there in Indiana somewhere. He come back, he couldn't hardly get a job so I told him, I said, Why don't you go in the Army for two years. And put -- tell them you want to be a truck driver, just explain it. So he went in the Army, and I never will forget, he went to -- transferred, went to Germany, and he was just a PFC or a corporal, you know, and he talked to them, they put him in the motor pool. And they had these old sergeants and he told them he was a truck driver, and he was. He was good because my brothers helped teach him. He wanted to be a first-class truck driver so he was. Anyways, he -- them sergeants told him, You said you're a truck driver? He said, Yeah. They had a big eighteen-wheeler out there and they just had space for parking between two others. He said, let's see if you can back that truck in there, and my son said he went out there and whipped it in and backed it in, because that's what he wanted to do, and he said he messed them sergeants up. They didn't know what to think when he backed it in there. So from then on he had it made driving a truck over there. So he got out, he went in the trucking business --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: -- got married and his wife went into the trucking business with him, driving.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And then he was hauling used cars out of Houston and New Orleans and he found out what they were -- what the price -- what the car sales were making, so he went into the car business and he's got three car lots here in San Anton.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Does he really?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Owns three big car lots. His son's working in the car lot. He's got a big, big place up at the lake, got a big home, he's a millionaire.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: He hit sixty-one the other day.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, did he? Wow.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But he -- there for a few years, that driving that truck when he came in, I told my wife -- she was worried about him the way he looked, been driving day and night, because that's what he wanted to do. So he hit the jackpot.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: So, yeah, and right now are you and your wife -- are you still out on the family farm?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: My wife passed away.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh, she did.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Passed away about 20 years ago.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Twenty years?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: She had that -- what do you call it -- starts with a P -- pancreatic cancer.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Yeah, you see in the paper a lot of women, I don't know why, it just ends up with women.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Oh that's too bad. But you are still out on the family farm, right?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: No, I was living out in Highland Hills.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Highland Hills?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Been doing -- DOC, doing work out on the farm.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: And I done did have, after I came here to this -- what do you call this -- assisted --

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Assisted living?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: But the reason I ended up at assisted living, I was out at the doctors after a few times and this lady -- lady doctor I had for about eight or ten years, she was pretty nice, you know. She told them I'm going to send you downstairs to the basement. I was, What for? She said, I want to run a test on you. So I went down there and they strapped me down, all that junk on your head and everything. I was there about thirty minutes and the lady down there and the guy that took the test, they said, You can go back up there to the office. And I got back up and the lady doc said, You need to wait about 20 or 30 minutes until I get the results. So they got the results. She said, Well, she said, You ain't going to like the results. I said, What do you mean? She said, I got to tell you, you should quit driving.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I said, Ain't nothing wrong with my driving. Guess what happened? Next week I got in a damn wreck. So I -- I decided that test -- I started thinking if I run into some family and injury a couple of young kids I could never live with myself, so I just quit driving.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah?

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I could most probably still drive, but if I happen -- I most almost probably couldn't live with it if I ended a couple of little kids.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: And there's plenty of crazy drivers out there in Texas anyway. You've got to watch out for them, too.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: Talk about crazy. They shouldn't allow a bunch of them from across the deals driving over here. It ain't even safe sometimes.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Yeah. Well, Lawrence, I thank you very much for sharing all your experience.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I enjoyed the catching-up session.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Well, you have a great memory and we thank you for your service, and thank you for sharing your story with us. And so, with that --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: What do you do with it? File 13?

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: No. It's going to get filed in the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: I think I covered everything, I guess. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: Okay. If there's anything -- if you think of anything else we can add it on, but otherwise --

sp.speaker: Lawrence McCulloch
sp.p: What am I supposed to do now?

sp.speaker: Kristin Anderson
sp.p: -- we can go ahead and wrap it up.
